strengths: Significant dataset contribution: PETAR-11K is the first large-scale PET/CT dataset with 11,356 lesion-level descriptions paired with 3D segmentation masks and structured annotations, addressing a genuine gap in medical imaging resources

Well-motivated architecture design with elegant solutions to domain challenges: focal prompting mechanism effectively addresses information loss from small lesions (<1% of volume), and additive mask conditioning provides clean integration of spatial information

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: multiple metric categories (NLP, semantic, LM-based), human evaluation by board-certified nuclear medicine physicians, correlation analysis identifying clinically-aligned metrics, and detailed ablation studies demonstrating component contributions

Strong and consistent empirical results: PETAR-4B outperforms all baselines across metrics with substantial improvements in clinically-relevant measures (CIDEr +0.283, GREEN +0.175) indicating superior content diversity and clinical reasoning quality

Thoughtful problem formulation demonstrating deep domain understanding: paper articulates specific PET challenges (volumetric complexity, dispersed small lesions, lengthy/variable reports) and addresses them systematically through design choices
weaknesses: Critical evaluation limitation: Single-institution evaluation severely constrains generalization claims. No cross-institutional validation despite known variations in PET reporting styles, protocols, and equipment across centers—essential for clinical deployment

Dataset quality and extraction pipeline transparency issues: mask generation via simple iterative thresholding lacks validation; no inter-rater agreement analysis; exact LLM prompts and filtering criteria relegated to supplementary material; no manual spot-checking of extracted descriptions against original reports

Potential train/test data contamination: pretraining on TotalSegmentator applied to the same CT volumes as downstream task may cause data leakage; train/test split methodology (patient-level vs. exam-level) not clearly specified

Limited technical novelty: mask-aware conditioning directly extends Reg2RG from 2D to 3D; focal prompting closely follows cited prior work [8,13]; four-stage training is standard practice. Architecture is primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques rather than methodologically novel

Incomplete robustness analysis: no evaluation of performance degradation with imperfect upstream lesion detection masks; no sensitivity analysis for focal prompt perturbation magnitude; no systematic error analysis or failure mode discussion; only 2 qualitative examples in Figure 4, with unexplained anatomical misclassification in first example

Experimental limitations undermine claims: single experimental run without confidence intervals or variance estimates; potentially suboptimal baseline adaptations (Med3DVLM performs suspiciously poorly at 0.004 BLEU); human evaluation limited (100 pairs in first round, 80 assessments in second); no inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) reported

Limited generalization scope: only 4 PET radiotracers covered despite many more in clinical use; no cross-tracer validation; unclear how well model generalizes to body regions beyond those in training; structured text format (region, organ, subsite, report) may artificially simplify task

Reproducibility and practical deployment concerns: dataset public availability not confirmed; proprietary model dependencies (Qwen3-30B-A3B) without specified checkpoints; no code release mentioned; critical details in supplementary material; inference time, memory footprint, and deployment feasibility not discussed; training requires 20 hours on specialized GPUs

strengths: Addresses an understudied and clinically important problem: PET/CT report generation in medical VLMs
Large-scale dataset contribution (PETAR-11K with 11,356 lesion descriptions from 5,000+ exams) claimed to be first of its kind with lesion-level granularity and 3D masks
Comprehensive evaluation framework including 8 automated metrics, human evaluation by board-certified physicians, correlation analysis, and ablation studies
Focal prompt mechanism directly addresses a genuine technical challenge (lesions occupying <1% of volume) with clear ablation evidence of its contribution
Clear documentation of dataset construction pipeline combining rule-based filtering and LLM extraction
Consistent improvements across metrics when all components are combined, demonstrating synergistic design
weaknesses: Dataset quality not validated: automated extraction via multiple LLMs lacks inter-model agreement metrics, validation accuracy reporting, or manual verification. Lesion mask generation via simple iterative thresholding (SUVmax ±0.1) is unvalidated

Limited technical novelty: straightforward combination of existing components (M3D encoder, Phi-3B LLM, additive mask conditioning). Focal prompting directly borrowed from concurrent work (FineCaption, Describe Anything)

Insufficient human evaluation: Round 1 uses only 100 lesion pairs; Round 2 evaluates only ~40 lesions across 5 physicians. No inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) reported. Evaluation criteria relegated to supplementary material

Experimental design gaps: test set construction from PETAR-11K not clearly described (train/val/test split undefined); risk of data leakage. No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. Unfair baseline comparisons (2D/CT models vs. PET-specific model)

Robustness and clinical applicability concerns: model assumes perfect lesion masks; no evaluation with real segmentation errors. Generated output is structured schema, not free-text reports (conversion to clinical format 'remains future work'). No end-to-end pipeline evaluation
Single-institution, limited-scope data: all data from one source with unknown generalization. Limited radiotracer diversity (4 tracers). No cross-validation or multi-site evaluation

Ablation study inconsistencies: baseline without masks/focal/CT achieves 0.485 BLEU (matches M3D-RAD finetuned), suggesting unclear configuration. Why does focal prompt alone improve more than combined CT+mask?

Metric correlation insights unexplored: Table 5 shows GREEN correlates 0.608 with human judgment but BLEU only 0.304—suggesting traditional NLP metrics fail for clinical evaluation. Paper doesn't discuss which metrics matter or explain the discrepancy

Reproducibility limitations: data release status ambiguous (privacy/IRB concerns not fully addressed). No code availability mentioned. Hyperparameters in supplementary material only. Inference cost not discussed

Missing critical analyses: no error analysis or failure cases; no per-lesion or body-region performance breakdown; handling of multi-lesion scans unclear; no computational cost comparison with baselines

strengths: Addresses important clinical gap: First work applying mask-aware VLMs to 3D volumetric PET/CT with explicit lesion localization, a challenging modality previously underexplored

Significant dataset contribution: PETAR-11K comprises 11,356 lesion descriptions with 3D segmentations from 5,000+ exams—the first such multimodal PET/CT dataset with lesion-level granularity, multiple radiotracers, and structured annotations

Well-engineered data pipeline: Intelligent hybrid approach combining rule-based filtering, RadGraph, and LLM ensembles (Mistral/Mixtral/Dolphin) effectively extracts structured lesion information from unstructured clinical reports

Comprehensive evaluation framework: Multiple metric categories (NLP, semantic, language-model based), human evaluation by board-certified physicians, broad baseline comparisons, thorough ablations, and introduction of PETAR-Bench establish rigorous assessment

Sound technical design: Focal prompt mechanism directly addresses key insight that lesions occupy <1% of volume; 4-stage progressive training pipeline is well-motivated; additive mask conditioning integrates multimodal inputs naturally

Strong empirical results: Achieves 29% BLEU improvement over InternVL3, substantial CIDEr (+0.283) and GREEN (+0.175) gains over M3D-RAD, with ablation studies validating each component's contribution
Valuable evaluation insights: Human evaluation reveals GREEN metric correlates best (ρ=0.608) with expert judgment, providing guidance for future medical report generation evaluation
Practical clinical perspective: Explicitly acknowledges system role in workflow using existing segmentation models or point-and-click annotation tools
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Components are largely assembled from existing techniques—additive mask conditioning is straightforward, focal prompts adapted from prior work, architecture reuses M3D encoder and standard LLMs. Primary contribution is dataset and problem formulation rather than novel methodology

Insufficient dataset quality validation: Automated mask generation via thresholding lacks validation against gold-standard manual annotations; LLM-based text processing (Qwen3-30B) introduces unvalidated processing step; no inter-rater agreement metrics for annotation quality; generalization characteristics (single/multi-institution) unclear

Evaluation limitations: Test set of 1,170 lesions with no confidence intervals or significance testing; human evaluation limited to 100 pairs (round 1) and 16 lesions per expert (round 2) without inter-rater reliability statistics; Med3DVLM's extremely poor performance (BLEU 0.004) suggests implementation issues; no stratified analysis by lesion characteristics or radiotracer

Missing critical experimental details: Train/validation/test splits not explicitly specified; hyperparameter selection process and sensitivity analysis absent; data augmentation strategies undocumented; inference time and memory requirements not reported; heavy reliance on supplementary material not provided for review

Incomplete robustness analysis: No failure case analysis or systematic error characterization; sensitivity to segmentation errors not addressed; no cross-dataset generalization evaluation; no performance stratification by lesion size, location, SUVmax, or anatomical region; Figure 4 examples appear cherry-picked

Generalization concerns: Evaluation limited to PET/CT; transferability to other 3D modalities (MRI, CT) unclear; potential single-institution or limited dataset source not confirmed; performance not stratified despite dataset including multiple radiotracers and anatomical regions

Reproducibility issues: Dataset release plan not explicitly confirmed despite claiming 'first publicly available'; code availability not mentioned; preprocessing pipeline dependencies on multiple external LLMs (Mistral, Mixtral, Dolphin, Qwen3) add complexity; four-stage training with selective freezing potentially sensitive to hyperparameters

Incomplete system design: Discussion acknowledges work is 'just a piece of the PETAR framework' with full clinical deployment requiring additional LLM post-processing deferred to future work; disconnect between lesion-level findings generation and comprehensive clinical report generation not addressed

Statistical rigor lacking: No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance testing of improvements; ablation study gains not tested for statistical significance; human evaluation correlation (Table 5) based only on 100 pairs without confidence bounds
Unclear baseline comparison fairness: Fine-tuning details for different models not fully specified—unclear whether all baselines received equal opportunity to benefit from PETAR-11K training data

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: PET automated reporting is clinically significant yet severely underrepresented in medical VLM research

Novel and valuable dataset contribution: PETARSeg-11K is the first public dataset combining lesion-level textual findings, 3D segmentation masks, and whole-body PET/CT volumes (11,356 lesions from 5,126 exams)
First human evaluation of automated PET reporting by board-certified physicians, establishing correlations between automated metrics (GREEN ρ=0.592) and expert judgment
Thoughtfully designed architecture addressing PET-specific challenges: focal prompting for sub-0.1% volume lesions, mask-aware dual-modality encoding, and three-stage training strategy
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple metric categories (n-gram, semantic, LLM-based) with both internal and external validation on autoPET dataset
Strong empirical improvements over 2D and 3D baselines (e.g., GREEN +0.186 vs best 3D model, ROUGE +0.070 vs best 2D model)
Rigorous ablation study demonstrating contribution of each component; focal prompt provides largest impact
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement and thorough supplementary material including cohort statistics and implementation details
weaknesses: Mask input dependency without robustness validation: model requires pre-segmented lesions, but no experiments test performance with automated masks or noise injection. Practical deployment requires automated segmentation but this is unvalidated

Meaningful performance gap to clinical utility: human evaluation shows PETAR-4B (3.7–3.9) versus ground truth (4.3–4.4); physicians preferred human-written findings in 47% of cases, limiting clinical acceptability

Limited architectural novelty: components largely combine existing techniques (3D ViT from M3D, focal prompt adapted from Describe Anything Model, mask conditioning similar to Reg2RG). Main contribution is task-specific application rather than methodological innovation

Quantitative hallucination problem unaddressed: model hallucinates lesion size and SUVmax values; human evaluation explicitly excluded these errors, yet they require manual correction in clinical workflow, reducing automation benefit

Modest dataset scale and limited generalization: 5,126 exams from single institution (2010–2013), single manufacturer (GE), four radiotracers only; external validation limited to 32 autoPET samples; temporal/center-specific bias possible

Insufficient human evaluation statistics: only 5 physicians with no inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's kappa), no confidence intervals or significance testing on preference statistics (116 sample size limits power)
Incomplete model comparisons: Pet2Rep (direct PET findings baseline) not compared; missing recent CT-based VLM comparisons; unclear whether PETAR's gains are due to architecture or dataset

Focal prompt design under-explored: random perturbation range (±20%) not justified; no ablation on magnitude; sensitivity to very small lesions (<0.01% volume) and cross-inference consistency not analyzed

Technical clarity gaps: spatial pooling operation not detailed; inference time/computational cost not reported; handling of multiple lesions per exam unclear; whether lesions have inter-lesion context

Missing error analysis and failure mode characterization: no systematic breakdown of which anatomical regions or lesion types are hardest; dataset mask generation (98% accuracy) has 2% error rate with unclear impact on model learning

strengths: First large-scale dataset (PETARSeg-11K) linking lesion-level PET/CT masks with free-text clinical findings—addresses genuine gap in medical AI research
Comprehensive evaluation including human study with 5 board-certified physicians and metric-human correlation analysis, revealing which metrics (GREEN, RaTEScore) align with clinical judgment
Well-motivated problem articulation: clearly explains why PET differs from CT (fine-grained descriptions, tiny lesions <0.1% volume, complex reporting)
Strong empirical improvements on clinically-relevant metrics: GREEN 3.6× and CIDEr 3.5× over M3D-RAD baseline
Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) systematically validate each component's contribution
External validation on AutoPET dataset demonstrates some generalization beyond training data
weaknesses: Lesion masks automatically generated via threshold-based algorithm (not manually verified); introduces unquantified training noise and undermines claims of dataset quality despite cited 98% accuracy from prior work

Limited technical novelty: focal prompting adapted from Describe Anything Model, mask conditioning via straightforward element-wise addition, architecture combines existing M3D + Phi3-4B components; three-stage training is standard transfer learning

Evaluation emphasizes metrics with weak human correlation: BLEU (ρ=0.214) and BARTScore (ρ=0.168) prominently reported in Table 2 despite negligible clinical predictive value; only GREEN (ρ=0.592) shows moderate correlation

Critical gap in human evaluation: PETAR scores 3.7–3.9 vs human 4.3–4.4; physicians preferred human reports in 40% of cases and tied in 47%—suggests outputs require significant revision; only 5 physicians and 148 total samples

Mask dependency contradicts automation claims: requires manual physician contours as input; no robustness analysis on segmentation errors; practical workflow requires additional manual bottleneck despite 'single-click' suggestions

Limited generalization: single institution, data from 2010–2013 (13+ years old), 93.6% FDG-PET with tiny minority of other tracers; external AutoPET validation only on 32 samples with undisclosed quantitative results

Incomplete methodology: three-stage training strategy not ablated; spatial pooling unexplained; 20% random perturbation range unjustified; why mask+focal alone provide such asymmetric improvements unexplored
Excluded quantitative measurements (size, SUVmax) from human evaluation despite their clinical criticality; acknowledged hallucinations not systematically addressed
Reproducibility concerns: dataset availability status unclear, no code release mentioned, some hyperparameter choices unexplained
Missing comparisons: Pet2Rep (concurrent work) cited but not compared; no simpler baselines; order-of-magnitude finetuning gain for Reg2RG (0.044→0.478 BLEU) unexplained

strengths: First large-scale public dataset (PETARSeg-11K) linking lesion-level PET/CT masks with free-text findings—addresses a genuine gap in medical imaging datasets with 11,356 lesions from 5,126 exams and 98% verified accuracy

Comprehensive evaluation including the first human study for automated PET report generation with 5 board-certified physicians, establishing novel correlations between automated metrics and expert judgment (GREEN ρ=0.59)
Strong empirical results with 3.6× improvement in GREEN score (0.257 vs 0.071) over finetuned M3D-RAD and 60% physician preference for PETAR findings
Well-motivated architectural design with thoughtful focal prompt mechanism for preserving fine-grained details of lesions occupying <0.1% of volume, validated through comprehensive ablation studies

Rigorous evaluation framework spanning multiple metric categories (n-gram, semantic, LLM-based) with external validation on autoPET dataset and responsible research practices (IRB approval, full anonymization)
weaknesses: Mask input dependency limits practical clinical deployment; no robustness evaluation under mask errors, contour inaccuracies, or variations in segmentation quality despite this being critical for real-world use

Limited architectural novelty—focal prompting adapted from Describe Anything Model, mask conditioning follows Reg2RG design, uses standard M3D transformer backbone; primary contribution is application rather than technical innovation

Human evaluation lacks critical rigor for medical studies: no inter-rater reliability coefficients (Cohen's κ, ICC) reported, only 5 physicians, quantitative measurements (SUVmax, lesion size) excluded due to hallucination but these are clinically important, and external evaluation limited to 32 samples

Inadequate systematic error analysis; no investigation of failure modes by lesion type, anatomical region, or radiotracer despite diverse dataset; Figure 4 shows selective examples without error distribution analysis

Dataset specificity concerns: data from 2010-2013 (13+ years old), predominantly FDG (94% of exams), limited coverage of other radiotracers; demographic information relegated to supplementary material; no analysis of dataset representativeness or biases

Statistical rigor gaps: no significance testing on quantitative comparisons, missing confidence intervals for human evaluation, focal prompt 20% perturbation magnitude appears arbitrary without ablation, no analysis of sensitivity to perturbation range

Unclear dataset accessibility and pretraining contribution: paper doesn't explicitly state PETARSeg-11K public release timeline; TotalSegmentator pretraining (100,000 samples) improvement shown in ablation but relative contribution quantification is unclear
